match.reason: The bank point Health literacy covers the whole skill set of finding, understanding, judging and using health information in general, while the new point is narrower and specific to judging nutrition information from qualified sources, evidence and quick-fix sales, so it is a related but broader card rather than the same idea.

draft.title: Judging nutrition information
card: Nutrition advice is everywhere, but not all of it is good. Students need to check where it comes from before trusting it.
Qualified source
Good advice comes from people with training in nutrition, such as an accredited practising dietitian, or from bodies such as the Department of Health.
Evidence
Good advice is backed by evidence, such as research that has been reviewed by other experts. A personal story or a before and after photo is not enough.
Quick fix
Be careful of advice that promises fast results, bans a whole food group or sells a product. Healthy eating is usually a steady habit, not a quick fix.
draft.remember: Trust advice from qualified sources, backed by evidence, with no quick fix.

a.q: Which piece of nutrition advice is the most reliable?
opts: A dietitian's advice based on reviewed research
A post that says a tea melts fat in three days
A friend's story about a diet that worked for them
An advertisement from a company selling the powder
a.why: A dietitian is a qualified source, and reviewed research is evidence. A friend's story is not enough evidence, and a fast fat loss claim and a seller's advertisement are signs of a quick fix.
a.clue: Look for training and evidence together.

b.q: Sam finds a website that says cutting out all carbohydrates fixes any health problem in a week. The site sells a meal plan. What is the best reason to doubt it?
opts: It promises a quick fix and sells a product
It talks about food, which is not a health topic
It is on a website, and websites are never reliable
It lists a week, and diets must last one month
b.why: A claim that one change fixes any problem in a week is a quick fix, and the site gains from selling its plan. A website can be reliable if it has qualified authors and evidence, so the website itself is not the problem.
b.clue: Ask who gains and how fast the results are promised.

a.best: A dietitian's advice based on reviewed research

b.best: It promises a quick fix and sells a product

problems.detail: The option 'An advertisement from a company selling the powder' says 'the powder' though no powder has been mentioned. It should say 'a powder' or name the product.

Three distractors are plainly absurd or use absolutes ('diets must last one month', 'websites are never reliable', 'food is not a health topic'). A student can rule them out without knowing the card's ideas, which leaves the right option standing out.

proposal.title: Judging nutrition information
card: Nutrition advice appears online, in shops and from friends. What matters is who wrote it and what it rests on, not where it appears.
Qualified source
Good advice comes from people with training in nutrition, such as an accredited practising dietitian, or from government health bodies.
Evidence
Good advice is backed by evidence, such as research that has been reviewed by other experts. A personal story or a before and after photo is not enough.
Quick fix

proposal.remember: Trust advice from qualified sources, backed by evidence, with no quick fix.

It is posted online rather than printed in a book
